The Problem
What happens when you make a scatterplot of species vs bill_depth_mm? What might be a better choice of geom?


The Solution

penguins |> 
    ggplot(mapping = aes(y = species, x = bill_length_mm)) + 
    geom_point() +

When creating a scatterplot, the points are split into the three different species categories, which is not very helpful when represented by a scatterplto. A boxplot can represent this relationship .

Question 6






NoteNote






The Problem
What does the na.rm argument do in geom_point()? What is the default value of the argument. Create a scatter plot where you successfully use this argument set to TRUE.


The Solution
na.rm determines whether points that have missing values create a warning that they were removed. The default value of the argument is FALSE.

title: First Steps
text:
Question 8






NoteNote






The Problem
Recreate the following visualization. What aesthetic should bill_depth_mm be mapped to? Should it be mapped at the global or geom level?


The Solution
bill_depth_mm should be mapped to color in the geom level, otherwise geom_smooth would be split by bill depth.

penguins |>
    ggplot(mapping = aes(y = body_mass_g, x = flipper_length_mm)) + 
    geom_point(mapping = aes(color = bill_depth_mm), na.rm = TRUE) +
    geom_smooth(method = "gam", na.rm = TRUE)

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ s(x, bs = "cs")'

title: First Steps
text:
Question 9






NoteNote






The Problem
Run this code in your head and predict what the output will look like. Then run the code and check your predictions.

ggplot(
  data = penguins,
  mapping = aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, color = island)
) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE)    



The Solution
I predict that the plot will have axes of body_mass_g vs flipper_length_mm. The points on the plot will be grouped with different by the island variable. There will be a linear model for each different island and the standard error of the estimated body mass at each value on the lines will not be visible.


`geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'









I predicted the components correctly, but I was not expecting the lines to overlap as much as they did.

title: First Steps
text:
Question 10






NoteNote






The Problem
Will these two graphs look different? Why/why not?

ggplot(
  data = penguins,
  mapping = aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)
) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth()

ggplot() +
  geom_point(
    data = penguins,
    mapping = aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    data = penguins,
    mapping = aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)
  )



The Solution
These plots will not look different. In the first plot, geom_point() and geom_smooth() inherit the mapping from ggplot(). In the second graph, the same mapping is explicity given to both functions.


`geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'









`geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'

Question 2






NoteNote






The Problem
How are the following two plots different? Which aesthetic, color or fill, is more useful for changing the color of bars?

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species)) +
  geom_bar(color = "red")







ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "red")










The Solution
The color aesthetic changes the border of the bars while fill changes the color of the whole bar. fill is the more useful option when changing bar colours.

Make a histogram of the carat variable in the diamonds dataset. Experiment with different binwidths. What binwidth reveals the most interesting patterns?

diamonds |>

    geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5)







diamonds |>

diamonds |>
    ggplot(aes(x = carat)) +
    geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.1)

title: Visualizing Relationships
text:
Question 2






NoteNote






The Problem
Make a scatterplot of hwy vs. displ using the mpg data frame. Next, map a third, numerical variable to color, then size, then both color and size, then shape. How do these aesthetics behave differently for categorical vs. numerical variables?


The Solution

mpg |> 
    ggplot(aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
    geom_point()







mpg |> 
    ggplot(aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = cty)) +
    geom_point()







mpg |> 
    ggplot(aes(x = displ, y = hwy, size = displ)) + 
    geom_point()







mpg |> 
    ggplot(aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = cty, size = displ)) +
    geom_point()









# Raises error due to passing a continous variable to shape
mpg |> 
    ggplot(aes(x = displ, y = hwy, shape = cty)) + 
    geom_point()

When the variable is categorical, all three aesthetics behave simillarly. Each category is assigned a unique color/size/shape.
When the variable is numerical, each of the aesthetics does something different:

color maps each value on a gradient, keeping all information.
size rounds each value to be one of a set of sizes with a positive integer value. It loses some information from the variable.
shape is unable to map to a numerical (continous) variable and raises an error when we attempt to map it.

title: Visualizing Relationships
text:
Question 4






NoteNote






The Problem
What happens if you map the same variable to multiple aesthetics?


The Solution

mpg |> 
  ggplot() + 
  geom_point(aes(x = hwy, y = hwy, color = hwy))







  mpg |> 
  ggplot() + 
  geom_point(aes(x = hwy, y = hwy, color = hwy, size = hwy))








When we map the same variable to multiple aesthetics (in scatterplots), The values follow a diagonal line, since for each point x and y are equal. For color and size, they became gradients with one extreme on one side of the line to the other extreme on the other end.

title: Visualizing Relationships
text:
Question 5






NoteNote






The Problem
Make a scatterplot of bill_depth_mm vs. bill_length_mm and color the points by species. What does adding coloring by species reveal about the relationship between these two variables? What about faceting by species.


The Solution

penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(color = species)) + 
  geom_point(
    aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm), 
    na.rm = TRUE)








This plot shows that the bill length and depth of the penguins measured are clustered by species.

penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(color = species)) + 
  geom_point(
    aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm), 
    na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~species)








When faceting by species, it is easier to see that Gentoo penguins have a noticible difference in bill depth to the other species and that Adelle penguins have a smaller bill length comapared to the other species.

title: Visualizing Relationships
text:
Question 6






NoteNote






The Problem
Why does the following yield two separate legends? How would you fix it to combine the two legends?

ggplot(
  data = penguins,
  mapping = aes(
    x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, 
    color = species, shape = species
  )
) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(color = "Species")

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).











The Solution
Two separate legends appear since our custom name for color is different that the default one for shape. We can fix it by either changing color back to the default legend name or change the name for shape to “Legend”.

ggplot(
  data = penguins,
  mapping = aes(
    x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, 
    color = species, shape = species 
  )
) +
  geom_point(na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(color = "Species", shape = "Species")

title: Visualizing Relationships
text:
Question 7






NoteNote






The Problem
Create the two following stacked bar plots. Which question can you answer with the first one? Which question can you answer with the second one?

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = island, fill = species)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill")







ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, fill = island)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill")










The Solution
The first plot (species vs island) shows for each island the proportion of penguins on that particular island. This plot can tell us what the population of each island look like. The second plot (island vs species) shows for each penguin species, the proportion of that species on each island. This plot can tell us the proportion of the total population of each penguin species across the different islands.

The Problem
Run the following lines of code. Which of the two plots is saved as mpg-plot.png? Why?

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class)) +

  ggplot(mpg, aes(x = cty, y = hwy)) +

Question 3






NoteNote






The Problem
Sort flights to find the fastest flights.


The Solution
We find the fastest flights by checking the difference in arrival and departure time. Since some flights are overnight, we need to account for rows with dep_time > arr_time to ensure we do not have negative flight times.

# Add a day (2400 minutes) if dep_time is later than arr_time
# This could produce errors if a flight took more than 24 hours (unrealistic) 
flights |> arrange((arr_time - dep_time) + 2400 * (dep_time > arr_time))

title: Rows
text:
Question 6






NoteNote






The Problem
Does it matter what order you used filter() and arrange() if you’re using both?


The Solution
It does matter in terms of computational cost. When you arrange first before you filter, we need to sort a larger number of rows compared to if you filter first. Since sorting has a larger computational cost \(O(n\cdot\log(n))\) (on average using quicksort) than filtering which has a cost of \(O(n)\). Thus we should do filtering first, the operation that is less ‘expensive’.

Question 7






NoteNote






The Problem
Why doesn’t the following work, and what does the error mean?

flights |> 
  select(tailnum) |> 
  arrange(arr_delay)
#> Error in `arrange()`:
#> ℹ In argument: `..1 = arr_delay`.
#> Caused by error:
#> ! object 'arr_delay' not found



The Solution
The issue is that during the select function call, we remove all columns except for tailnum, so when we try to arrange by arr_delay, it does not exist in the table we piped into it. To fix this issue, we just need to swap the order of select and arrange.

flights |> 
  arrange(arr_delay) |>
  select(tailnum)
